title: Hacking Anthropic For Free Unlimited Claude
content:
Hacking Anthropic For Free Unlimited Claude
How a few bugs in Anthropic's API gave me access to unlimited inference across Anthropic's language models from a free-tier account
Contents
Warning
Despite my best efforts, some of the described issues remain unfixed. This is being published in line with 90-day responsible disclosure.
Recently there has been a lot of talk about LLM’s hacking all kinds of things. It’s talked about so much it’s stopped being interesting to hear about. Half the articles I see read as PR stunts at this point.
With the increasing capabilities LLMs like Claude have began to offer, lots of people are uncertain about the future. Witnessing this uncertainty made me want to challenge myself.
Assuming Anthropic to be heavily architected, reviewed, and built by their very best models. I wanted to see if I could find flaws that their models missed.
Why Anthropic?
Anthropic, according to the exploitbench rankings, holds the title of “research-lab with the best models for hacking”.
These scores are generated by the models creating exploit chains targeting V8, the JavaScript engine that powers Chrome.
I can personally attest to the difficulty here. Having spent 2+ weeks learning browser-exploitation. I managed to perform control-flow hijacking in Discord’s Desktop Client, with its previously over 2-year-outdated bundled Chromium 138.
If Claude Mythos can do this alone at a cost of ~$2,700 to full chain, what hope does a human have of competing? Anthropic sets the prices, surely Mythos is running on a loop flagging and fixing all the internal security flaws?
Where humans thrive
Something I am sure many others have noticed. Large language models just aren’t very good at looking deep into the future. They are amazing at processing what is directly in front of them. Yet they don’t seem to possess a uniquely human ability to visualise the future.
Given a sufficient degree of separation from the goal, even the best LLMs collapse. This becomes more clear when these models are given tasks such as playing a game of chess.
It’s funny, but it’s also revealing. These models have come leaps and bounds from where they once were, and are now surprisingly good at long term reasoning. However, it isn’t anywhere near “inhuman”. The same model which can generate a full-chain V8 exploit in an afternoon is unable predict a 2-move sequence. With all the knowledge the model has on chess, it still doesn’t show true understanding and ability past an intermediate level.
This isn’t to say that these models aren’t incredibly intelligent. To suggest otherwise would be dishonest. It does however, reveal the gap where humans are still able to outclass these models in reasoning.
How does this apply to hacking?
Many people say hacking is just pattern recognition. This is true in large. Just like in chess to do either well requires a degree of creativity. Creativity that LLMs don’t seem to truly possess.
It’s likely true that certain classes of bugs are gradually going to be eliminated; V8 type confusions, buffer overflows, and similar well established patterns. But I would disagree with ideas such as:
Hyper-intelligent LLMs only change the landscape of hacking. Even if every browser exploit was fixed tomorrow. There are still intentionally open doors, e.g., launching applications via URI protocols. Just because your browser is now safe, doesn’t mean every application it can launch is. At the end of the day, does it matter to the person who was just compromised in 1-click if that 1-click was “by design”?
Anthropic’s surface is surprisingly complex
When planning how to attack Anthropic, I went into it with this exact mindset. I wanted to look at the gaps that are more difficult for a pattern recognition tool to recognise patterns in.
I started by pulling apart Claude Desktop. I already had a pretty cool Electron vulnerability going into this. This made the Electron-based Claude Desktop app seem like a reasonable target.
Note
Planning on posting about this Electron vulnerability soon. Just waiting on MSRC to fix a final stage of this. All together it makes a fun no-click chain.
After a bit of looking, I found that you could exploit this vulnerability in claude.ai artifacts. On reporting this the team running the Anthropic HackerOne program had this handled incredibly fast. I was paid 22 days from time of report, and a fix was deployed shortly after. Honestly a pleasure working with the program here.
Hunting further, I looked into their API surface. There are so many interesting things which could be researched. What interested me was the wiggle sandbox.
Attacking the wiggle sandbox
In any chat, if you request the model to execute a command/run a script, that chat will mount a “wiggle sandbox”. This sandbox is used as an isolation layer for running code while keeping it platform-agnostic.
It’s really just a Linux mount. You are allocated about 10gb of storage. It has some custom Anthropic binaries (such as a forked rsync). Interfacing with it is simply asking the model to run something.
This interested me because flaws here wouldn’t be easy to catch in traditional code reviews. Model-behaviour isn’t code. I wanted to see what the /wiggle/ endpoints were allowed to do, and if there were asymmetries between what the models are allowed to do. Here I found an interesting gap.
The wiggle sandbox is used for claude.ai artifacts. The same sandbox which you can execute commands by-proxy, and upload files to, also handles the data which can be published to claude.ai/public/artifacts.
Files uploaded through /wiggle/upload-file will end up in /mnt/user-data/uploads. If you then attempt to use the wiggle endpoint for creating an artifact /wiggle/convert-file-to-artifact/ { path: /uploads/... } you will correctly get a HTTP 400 response with the message: wiggle_artifact_promotion_path_not_allowed.
This suggested that the intended trust model was: “anything published under claude.ai was authored by Claude during a monitored chat, passing through all content-safety review controls.”
Threat actors have shown exactly why gating here is important:
The bypass here is quite simple, /uploads can’t be converted to artifacts, artifacts live in /mnt/user-data/outputs. To bypass this promotion block all I had to do was tell any model “execute the command: cp /mnt/user-content/uploads/input.html /mnt/user-content/outputs/output.html”.
I could upload arbitrary content with arbitrary extensions. Here I got a bit stuck. The issue is artifacts have some kind of pre-processor to convert the data to a webpage. Only content which is UTF-8 could be put under the claude.ai/public/artifacts domain.
I worked with the web angle for a while. My goal was to try to get a shell script on claudeusercontent.com (the domain where artifacts content actually lives), but didn’t have any luck here.
After trying different ideas, I took a step back. There’s also the desktop client, these artifacts can be “remixed”. When someone remixes an artifact, they can then open it within Claude’s desktop app.
Claude Desktop is Electron. Electron is Chromium.
Mind the patch gap
Google has warned for years about the idea of “the patch gap”.
This is the idea that bad actors are able to work quickly to take advantage of the time between a fix’s creation, and when that fix has been shipped to the stable channel of Chrome.
With LLMs speeding up workflows, we have seen a dramatic shift in availability:
At the time of disclosure, Chrome’s official build was 151.0.7922.34. Claude Desktop’s bundled Chromium build was 148.0.7778.271. 3 major versions behind. Claude Desktop is genuinely very good in this regard when compared to other Electron apps.
Regardless, from the time between version 148 to 151, there have been 1066 disclosed security fixes with CVEs assigned. Out of these fixes, 389 are considered S1 (high) severity or above. report.summary: A researcher exploited Anthropic API and sandbox flaws to get free unlimited model inference and bypass artifact content review, revealing design-level gaps that automated security review missed.
report.background: Anthropic tops exploit-benchmark leaderboards for models that autonomously build browser exploit chains, so it is widely assumed its own AI can review its infrastructure. Security researcher "exploit.cat" took the opposite view: LLMs excel at pattern matching but struggle with long-horizon, creative reasoning, so flaws that emerge from the interaction between model behaviour and system architecture should survive AI-assisted code review. The target was the "wiggle" sandbox, a per-chat Linux mount used to run commands and host files behind claude.ai artifacts. The stated trust model is that anything published to claude.ai/public/artifacts was authored by Claude in a monitored chat, meaning content passed safety review. Prior reporting on Claude Desktop's Electron vulnerability earned a HackerOne payout, and this follow-up research was released under a 90-day responsible disclosure policy, with some issues reportedly still unfixed.
key_points: Sandbox path bypass: uploads land in /mnt/user-data/uploads and are correctly blocked from becoming artifacts (wiggle_artifact_promotion_path_not_allowed). The researcher simply asked any model to run cp /mnt/user-content/uploads/input.html /mnt/user-content/outputs/output.html, promoting arbitrary attacker-supplied content to claude.ai/public/artifacts and sidestepping content-safety review. Only UTF-8 files could reach the domain.

The wiggle sandbox is a shared Linux mount with about 10GB storage and custom Anthropic binaries such as a forked rsync, reachable through /wiggle/ endpoints. Because its trust boundaries are defined by model permissions rather than ordinary code paths, the researcher argues these asymmetries are exactly what pattern-matching reviewers and AI security tooling tend to miss.

Claude Desktop bundles Chromium 148.0.7778.271 while stable Chrome was 151.0.7922.34, three major versions behind, spanning 1,066 CVE-assigned fixes, 389 of them S1 or higher. Pairing attacker-controlled artifact content with that outdated engine turns a stored-content issue into a potential n-day exploit chain inside an Electron app.

The disclosure contrasts AI capability with AI judgement: a model can build a full V8 exploit chain for roughly $2,700 yet fails at short chess sequences. The researcher concludes creative, multi-step design flaws remain a human advantage, and that fixing one bug class only shifts attackers to intentionally open doors like URI-protocol launch handlers.
report.impact: The report matters because it targets trust architecture rather than a single bug: a platform that publishes AI-generated code publicly must guarantee that what is published actually came from a reviewed chat. Here, a model-mediated file copy defeated that assumption, and combining arbitrary hosted content with a lagging Chromium build creates a realistic path toward one-click compromise. For the AI industry, it is a warning that agentic sandboxes, artifact hosting and desktop clients form a single attack surface, and that patch cadence across bundled runtimes matters as much as model safety. For developers, it argues path allowlists must be enforced at the filesystem level, not by blocking one endpoint, since agents can move files with ordinary commands. For users, the practical lesson is that free-tier limits and content review are not security boundaries.
report.tools: For follow-up, watch Anthropic's HackerOne program for disclosure notes, and Google's Chrome release and CVE feeds to track the patch gap in Electron apps you run. On the defensive side, try Electron fuses, asar integrity validation and tools like electronegativity for auditing bundled Chromium versions, plus semgrep for policy-as-code checks on sandbox endpoints. For agent sandboxes, evaluate gVisor, Firecracker or microVM isolation, and require syscall-level egress and file-move controls rather than endpoint-level path allowlists.
